articles.author: Sameer Mistry
articles.description:
Hey hunters  — I’m Sameer, maker of UniSin.
I built this because I kept meaning to post on LinkedIn and then… not posting. The native composer is fine for one update. It is terrible if you want a week of posts sitting in a queue and going out at a time you already picked.
The problem I was solving: stay consistent without living in LinkedIn, and without using scrapers or “engagement bots” that get accounts restricted. UniSin uses LinkedIn’s official API only. You add a date and time, write the post, and it publishes when the slot is due.
What changed while building it: I started with fancy schedule templates. What I actually needed was simpler — pick a day, pick a time, put a post in that slot, see the queue. Also learned the hard way that “scheduled” and “published” are not the same as “the clock hit that time.” If the worker is not running, the post just sits there. So the product is honest about that: official API, visible queue, you can still hit Post now.
It’s open source and I’m using it on my own profile.
Live: https://unisin.in
https://github.com/Sameermistrii/Linkdin_Automation
If you try it, tell me what broke. That is more useful than a generic “congrats on the launch.”
articles.title: UniSin - LinkdIn Post Scheduler

articles.author: xxxn3m3s1sxxx
articles.description:
Your Rust Code Proves You Don't Understand Memory


You chose Rust because the internet told you it was the future. Now your codebase is 6x longer and you still cannot ship.
The borrow checker is not a feature. It is a gatekeeper that charges you in hours.
You spend more time fighting the compiler than writing actual logic. The lifetime annotations pile up. The reference rules multiply. The code becomes a maze of ownership transfers that nobody can follow.
That signature is not safety. That is a subscription model for your time.
Rust promises safety. What it delivers is a productivity tax that nobody admits to paying.
Compilation time: Your Rust project takes 5 minutes to compile. Your Go project takes 5 seconds.
Learning curve: Junior devs spend months learning lifetimes instead of shipping features.
Code length: Simple operations become 10x longer with ownership annotations.
Rust is excellent for:
Systems programming
Performance-critical code
Embedded devices
WebAssembly
Rust is terrible for:
CLI tools
CRUD applications
Quick prototypes
Anything where development speed matters more than runtime speed
Your borrow checker obsession is a personality trait, not a technical choice.
If you cannot explain why you need Rust for your specific use case, you are probably using it wrong.
What has been your experience with Rust? Share your thoughts in the comments.
articles.title: Your Rust Code Proves You Don't Understand Memory
